title: The Journey of Lautaro: From the Stable of the Conqueror to the Gates of Santiago
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: Tirúa country, coast of Arauco, birthplace under the Nahuelbuta
stops.campa: A boy is born in the country of Tirúa, where the Nahuelbuta range walks down into the sea, son of the lonko Curiñancu. They name him Leftraru: the swift hawk, the traro that stoops faster than sight. The machis read the bird in him: a thing that circles high, watches long, and falls once. The land he opens his eyes on is the land the huincas have not yet touched; south of the Bío-Bío the rehues stand as they have stood since the world was ordered. He is born already belonging to the war that has not yet begun.
suggested_refs: Pablo Neruda, 'Educación del cacique' (Canto General): 'Lautaro era una flecha delgada'
Monolith to Lautaro at Tirúa

stops.name: Slopes of the Nahuelbuta cordillera, the boyhood
stops.campa: The boy grows in the mountain of the tigers, Nahuelbuta, among araucarias and mist. He learns what a lonko's son learns: the sling, the lance-play of the palin field, the memory-threads of lineage, the silence of the hunter. The elders say the hawk-child could stand a whole morning watching the condors work the wind, learning how a thing without weight defeats a thing with weight. North of the great river, in these same years, Pedro de Valdivia founds Santiago and writes to his King that there is no better land in the world. The two lives are already moving toward each other.
suggested_refs: Neruda, 'Educación del cacique', the whole poem is this boyhood
Nahuelbuta National Park, the standing araucarias
sources: Jerónimo de Vivar, Crónica y relación copiosa y verdadera de los reynos de Chile (1558)

stops.name: Quilacura, before the Bío-Bío: the capture
stops.campa: Valdivia probes toward the Bío-Bío with sixty horse, and at Quilacura in the night the lances of the south meet Spanish cavalry for the first time. In the raids of these entradas the boy of Tirúa, some eleven years old, is taken. The canon is exact about the wound and vague about the day: a child roped among the yanaconas, marched north, away from the great river of his country, the frontier he will spend his whole life fighting back toward. The hawk is caged. The Spaniards do not know what they are carrying back to Santiago in their baggage-train.
suggested_refs: Neruda, 'Lautaro entre los invasores' (Canto General)
Battle of Quilacura in Vivar's Crónica
sources: Jerónimo de Vivar, Crónica, caps. sobre la entrada de 1546

stops.name: Santiago del Nuevo Extremo, Valdivia's stables
stops.campa: In Santiago the boy is given to the governor's own service: yanacona and groom, keeper of Pedro de Valdivia's horses. He carries water, oils leather, holds the stirrup of the conqueror of Chile. The Spaniards call him Felipe. But the stable is a school. He learns that the horse is not a monster but an animal that fears, tires, founders in soft ground; he learns its feeding, its shoeing, the number of leagues it can make and the hour at which it can make no more. The canon says it plainly: in the shadow of Valdivia, Lautaro studies Valdivia.
suggested_refs: Neruda, 'Lautaro entre los invasores': 'Atendió las armas del capitán... vio arder las lanzas'
Plaza de Armas de Santiago, ground of the first city
sources: Alonso de Góngora Marmolejo, Historia de todas las cosas que han acaecido en el Reino de Chile (1575)

stops.name: Santiago, the school of war
stops.campa: Riding at his master's side on escort and muster, the page watches everything: how the harquebus is charged and how long it takes to charge again; how the cavalry forms and where a squadron of horse cannot go; how the Spaniards, so few, keep so many in obedience: by order, by terror, and by the horse. He learns Castilian and keeps Mapudungun beneath it like a knife under a cloak. The soldiers find the young groom quick, silent, useful. Valdivia trusts him near his person. The canon savors the irony: the conqueror himself is arming his destroyer, lesson by lesson.
suggested_refs: Pedro Subercaseaux's historical canvases of the Conquest
The figure of 'Felipe Lautaro' in the crónicas
sources: Pedro Mariño de Lobera, Crónica del Reino de Chile

stops.name: The road south, Valdivia's great entrada
stops.campa: Valdivia marches south with two hundred Spaniards and their yanaconas to conquer the country beyond the Itata, and the groom Felipe rides in his train, returning toward his own land in the enemy's livery. Every league is a lesson in logistics: the trains of pack-horses, the fords, the order of camp and sentinel. The boy who left Arauco roped in a baggage-train comes back watching the invading army from inside its own skin, counting its horses, measuring the exact width of its shadow. The Bío-Bío country rises around him like a memory returning blood to a numb limb.
suggested_refs: Valdivia's cartas to Charles V on the 1550 campaign
sources: Pedro de Valdivia, Cartas de relación (carta de 15 de octubre de 1550)

stops.name: River Andalién, the night battle
stops.campa: By the Andalién, in the dark, Ainavillo hurls the massed levies of Arauco against Valdivia's camp, the first great battle of the war. The boy holds horses behind the line and hears his own people's war-cries for the first time since his capture; he sees them break at last against cavalry and shot, spears against powder. He sees also what the Spaniards do not see: that the squadrons came all at once, spent themselves in one wave, and had nothing behind. In the ashes of that night the whole military thought of Lautaro is quietly conceived: never again one wave.
suggested_refs: Battle of Andalién in Vivar's Crónica
Valdivia's own account in his carta of October 1550
sources: Pedro de Valdivia, Cartas de relación

stops.name: Fort of Penco, the mutilation of the prisoners
stops.campa: After the assault on the new fort at Penco is broken, Valdivia sits in judgment on his prisoners. The sentence is recorded by his own chronicler: hands and noses cut from some two hundred men of Arauco, the maimed sent home as living letters of the King's justice. The boy Felipe stands in the governor's service and watches the axe fall, and fall, and fall. The canon marks this day as the wound that never closes: what the Spaniards intend as terror, the hawk receives as instruction. He looks at the man whose stirrup he holds and finishes his studies.
suggested_refs: Vivar's Crónica, the mutilations after Andalién and Penco
Neruda, 'Se desata el corazón vengador' (Canto General)
sources: Jerónimo de Vivar, Crónica y relación copiosa y verdadera

stops.name: Concepción del Nuevo Extremo (Penco), the conqueror's new city
stops.campa: Valdivia founds Concepción on the bay of Penco, doorway to the conquest of the south, and the groom serves through its first raisings: palisade, church, the branding of encomiendas. Southward the new forts go up: Arauco, Tucapel, Purén, each a nail driven into the body of his homeland. Lautaro tends the horses of the men who ride out to collect tribute and rides among them, memorizing garrisons, distances, the seasons when the fords run low. The canon gives him these months as a spy given his commission by God: nothing he sees is wasted, and he sees everything.
suggested_refs: Foundation of Concepción, October 1550
The line of forts: Arauco, Tucapel, Purén

stops.name: Out of the Spanish lines, the escape
stops.campa: On a day the chronicles do not fix (the canon says only that it came when he had learned all there was to learn), Felipe the groom vanishes from the Spanish service. A horse-boy missing; a matter for a shrug. He goes south through the fog country of Arauco, shedding the Spanish name on the trail like a snake's skin, carrying invisible contraband: cavalry drill, powder-times, the terror-economy of the conquest, the face of Valdivia. The hawk has slipped the jesses. Every Spaniard he passes on the road is a dead man who does not know it yet.
suggested_refs: Neruda: 'Lautaro regresó a su gente', 'El invasor había regresado'
Memoria Chilena, the escape c. 1550-52

stops.name: Tirúa, the homecoming
stops.campa: He comes back to his father's hearth a man of eighteen who left as a child of eleven, speaking his own tongue with the ghost of Castile in it. Around the fires of Curiñancu's ruca he tells the country what he has brought: that the huinca dies like any man; that the horse is a servant that can change masters; that the thunder-weapon is slow between one thunder and the next; that the invincibility of the invader is a story the invader tells. The lonkos listen. The young men look at him the way men look at weather coming. Word travels along the coast: the hawk has returned knowing.
suggested_refs: Neruda, 'El caudillo' (Canto General)
Statue of Lautaro, Plaza de Cañete

stops.name: Valley of Arauco, the great council
stops.campa: The lonkos of the sixteen ayllarehues gather in council, and the canon of the nation was written for this scene: the caciques quarrel over who shall bear the toqui's stone axe, until old Colocolo rises, 'ancient in years, and in wisdom more ancient,' the poem says, and turns their fury outward, ordaining the trial of the tree-trunk by which Caupolicán, who bears the log three days and nights, is raised toqui. And into that same order of war the returned hawk is received: Lautaro, who knows the enemy from inside, made lieutenant of the toqui, keeper of the new war. The assembly drinks and swears.
stops.quote: Caciques, del Estado defensores, / codicia de mandar no me convida / a pesarme de veros pretensores / de cosa que a mí tanto era debida; / porque, según mi edad, ya veis, señores, / que estoy al otro mundo de partida; / mas el amor que siempre os he mostrado / a bien aconsejaros me ha incitado.
stops.quote_source: Colocolo's speech, La Araucana, Canto II
suggested_refs: La Araucana, Canto II, Colocolo's speech, praised by Voltaire above Homer's Nestor
Rubén Darío, sonnet 'Caupolicán'
The log-trial of Caupolicán in painting and schoolbook
sources: Alonso de Ercilla, La Araucana, Canto II

stops.name: Clearings of the Nahuelbuta, the new war invented
stops.campa: In hidden clearings Lautaro builds the army that has never existed before. He breaks the old single wave into relays: squadrons that fight, retire, breathe, and return, so the battle never rests: a mill to grind cavalry. He teaches the feigned flight that draws horsemen onto broken ground; the lasso and the pike-hedge against the charge; captured horses ridden by Mapuche riders, the first native cavalry of the Indies. He chooses ground as a weapon: swamp, ravine, forest edge. The elders watch the boy drill the levies with Spanish patience and Mapuche fury, and understand that something new has entered the world.
suggested_refs: Ercilla's portrait: 'Fue Lautaro industrioso, sabio, presto' (Canto III)
Encina and Barros Arana on Lautaro as military innovator
sources: Alonso de Ercilla, La Araucana, Canto III

stops.name: Fort of Tucapel: the rising begins
stops.campa: The signal runs the ridge-lines. The country around the fort of Tucapel goes silent: tribute stops, messengers vanish, the yanaconas melt away; and then the storm: the garrison, ambushed and harried, spikes what it cannot carry and falls back on Purén. The Mapuche burn the fort and Lautaro camps his squadrons in the ashes, on the loma of Tucapel, and waits. He has chosen this ground with a groom's eye for what kills horses: rough approaches, tired mounts arriving uphill, no field for a charge to gather weight. The trap is the place itself. He sends Valdivia the silence as an invitation.
suggested_refs: Site of Fuerte Tucapel, Cañete
Góngora Marmolejo on the abandonment of Tucapel
sources: Alonso de Góngora Marmolejo, Historia de Chile, caps. XIII-XIV

stops.name: The road from Purén: Valdivia summoned
stops.campa: Pedro de Valdivia, conqueror of Chile, rides out from Concepción to punish the rising with some fifty Spaniards and his auxiliaries, gathering ill omens as he comes: scouts who do not return, heads set on the trail, the messenger Luis de Bobadilla's party swallowed whole by the quiet country. The canon gives him the arrogance of the doomed: he keeps Christmas Eve in the saddle, marching on Tucapel to relieve a fort that no longer exists. On the loma, Lautaro disposes his squadrons in the forest and rehearses the relays one last time. He knows exactly who is coming. He groomed his horse for years.
suggested_refs: Góngora Marmolejo, caps. on Valdivia's last march
La Araucana, Canto III, the omens of the road
sources: Alonso de Góngora Marmolejo, Historia de Chile
Alonso de Ercilla, La Araucana, Canto III

stops.name: Loma of Tucapel: the battle, Christmas Day
stops.campa: Christmas morning, 1553. Valdivia reaches the burned fort and the forest opens. Squadron after squadron comes on in Lautaro's relays: fighting, retiring, replaced, unending, until Spanish arms grow too heavy to lift and the horses stand blown. When the last counter-charge wavers, the canon gives the day its axis: the young toqui rises and hurls his voice at the wavering squadrons, and the field turns. By evening the fifty are dead, the yanaconas destroyed, and the invincibility of Spain lies on the loma with them. It is the first time in the New World that a native army has annihilated a Spanish governor's force in open battle.
stops.quote: ¡Oh ciega gente, del temor guiada! / ¿A dó volvéis los temerosos pechos? [...] a lo menos firmad el pie ligero, / a ver cómo en defensa vuestra muero.
stops.quote_source: Lautaro's harangue at Tucapel, La Araucana, Canto III
suggested_refs: La Araucana, Canto III, the arenga of Lautaro
Memoria Chilena, 'Batalla de Tucapel'
Mural and monument tradition of Tucapel/Cañete
sources: Alonso de Ercilla, La Araucana, Canto III

stops.name: Pilmaiquén clearing, the death of Pedro de Valdivia
stops.campa: Valdivia flees with the priest Pozo, is mired, taken, and brought bound before the victors. The canon keeps every version of what follows, and holds them all true at once: Vivar says Caupolicán sentenced him and his head went onto a lance; Góngora Marmolejo says they cut his forearms with clam-shells, roasted and ate them before his living eyes; Mariño de Lobera gives the death-blow to Leucotón's mace; and the folk tradition pours molten gold down the conqueror's throat, saying: drink the thirst you came with. He offers to empty Chile of Spaniards for his life. The answer of Arauco is the sentence carried out.
suggested_refs: Neruda, 'El corazón de Pedro de Valdivia' (Canto General)
The molten-gold tradition
Góngora Marmolejo cap. XIV; Vivar cap. CXV; Mariño de Lobera
sources: Jerónimo de Vivar, Crónica, cap. CXV
Alonso de Góngora Marmolejo, Historia de Chile, cap. XIV
Pedro Mariño de Lobera, Crónica del Reino de Chile

stops.name: Camp of the victors, Tucapel valley: the hawk confirmed
stops.campa: In the victory camp the nation takes the measure of its instrument. The poem itself pauses over him here, as the army does: young, composed, neither tall nor short, courteous of face and iron underneath: a general of twenty who has just killed the conqueror of a kingdom. Caupolicán confirms him lieutenant-general of the war with his own command of squadrons. The severed head of Valdivia travels the rehues as proof and sacrament. Around the fires the young men repeat the new catechism: they die; their horses obey us; the war can be won. Fourteen thousand levies answer the summons for the campaign to come.
stops.quote: Fue Lautaro industrioso, sabio, presto, / de gran consejo, término y cordura.
stops.quote_source: Ercilla's portrait of Lautaro, La Araucana, Canto III
suggested_refs: Ercilla's octave-portrait of Lautaro, Canto III
Statue of Lautaro at Cañete plaza
sources: Alonso de Ercilla, La Araucana, Canto III

stops.name: Cuesta de Marigüeñu: Villagra's column destroyed
stops.campa: Francisco de Villagra comes south from Concepción with a hundred and fifty-odd Spaniards, six field-pieces, and the honor of Spain to avenge. Lautaro lets him climb. On the wooded heights of Marigüeñu, above the Chivilingo, he has cut trenches, laid abatis, and posted his relays; when the column is committed on the slope the squadrons close like a fist. The guns are taken, the horses useless on the grade, the retreat a running slaughter to the ford: barely half the force staggers back alive, leaving artillery, baggage and eighty-eight Spaniards in Mapuche hands. Ever after the Spaniards name the mountain for the beaten man: Cuesta de Villagrán.
suggested_refs: La Araucana, Cantos V-VI, Marigüeñu
The toponym 'Cuesta de Villagrán' itself
Memoria Chilena, 'Batalla de Marigüeñu'
sources: Alonso de Ercilla, La Araucana, Cantos V-VI

stops.name: Concepción, the first destruction
stops.campa: Word of Marigüeñu reaches Concepción ahead of the army, and the city empties: men, women, and the memory of Valdivia's capital streaming north toward Santiago. Lautaro enters a city of shut doors and burning larders. The squadrons take what war can use (iron, cloth, horses, wine) and give the rest to fire. The bell that rang the conquest's masses falls into ash. The canon lingers on the image: the yanacona groom standing in the plaza of the city he helped his master build, watching it return to the earth of Penco. He does not garrison it. He is not building an empire; he is unbuilding one.
suggested_refs: La Araucana, Canto VII, the flight and the sack
Doña Mencía de los Nidos, who shamed the fleeing citizens (Ercilla)
sources: Alonso de Ercilla, La Araucana, Canto VII
Alonso de Góngora Marmolejo, Historia de Chile

stops.name: Return across the Bío-Bío, the quiet year
stops.campa: The army goes home laden, and then the other invader arrives: the one no squadron can relay against. Chavalongo, the burning fever, walks the rukas of Arauco; smallpox follows; the fields, unsown in the war year, give famine for harvest. The dead of the plague outnumber the dead of all the battles. Lautaro disperses the levies to their lineages and holds the alliance together through the dying season with messengers and patience. The canon reads the pestilence as the price of the head of Valdivia, and notes that the toqui pays it without releasing his grip on the purpose: Santiago.
suggested_refs: The chavalongo (typhus) of 1554-55 in the crónicas

segments.name: The Plague and the Second Fire

stops.name: Arauco heartland, holding the people through the pestilence
stops.campa: A second year of sickness and hunger. Lonkos who swore at the great council now count their dead and mutter for peace; the machis drum against a plague that came in the invaders' blood and stayed after their forts burned. Lautaro rides lineage to lineage, keeping the confederation alive the way a man keeps a fire in rain, shielding it with his body. The canon gives him this hardest generalship, the kind without battles: to hold fourteen thousand grieving households to a war that must resume, because he alone has seen Santiago and knows the enemy will never stop coming on their own.
suggested_refs: Memoria Chilena on the epidemics of 1554-1555

stops.name: Penco: the Spaniards return to rebuild
stops.campa: The Audiencia of Lima orders Concepción raised again, and the settlers creep back to Penco to rebuild on the ashes: a wall, huts, a hope. Watchers on the ridges count them as they land. Lautaro summons the squadrons out of the plague-thinned country, and they come: four thousand who remember the relays. He moves on the city before its palisade has hardened, in the reasoning the canon attributes to him whole: a fort forgiven is a fort forever. The lesson of 1554 must be taught twice, so that Spain will understand it was not fortune. It was method.
suggested_refs: The Real Audiencia's rebuilding order, 1555
sources: Alonso de Góngora Marmolejo, Historia de Chile

stops.name: Concepción, the second destruction
stops.campa: The squadrons storm rebuilt Concepción. The defense breaks in hours; the garrison and settlers are cut down or driven into the sea, and the canon counts the survivors with terrible exactness: thirty-eight souls, saved by a ship standing off Penco while the second city of Chile burns behind them. Twice founded, twice ash. In Santiago the news lands like the tolling of a bell: the frontier no longer holds anywhere south of the Maule, and men say aloud that the Indian general means to come north. For once the fear of the settlers and the plan of the toqui are the same thing.
suggested_refs: Segunda destrucción de Concepción, 12 December 1555
La Araucana on the destructions of the city
sources: Alonso de Góngora Marmolejo, Historia de Chile

stops.name: Council at the Bío-Bío, the audacity resolved
stops.campa: On the north bank of the great river the toqui lays his design before the war-council, and it is the design no toqui has dared: not to defend Arauco but to end the conquest at its root, Santiago itself. Emissaries of the promaucaes have promised risings north of the Maule. The old men object that no army of the south has ever campaigned so far from its harvests; Lautaro answers with the map in his head, ford by ford: Itata, Ñuble, Maule, Mataquito, the groom's inventory of his master's house. The council grants him his picked squadrons. The hawk turns north.
suggested_refs: Memoria Chilena: the northern campaigns as unprecedented audacity

stops.name: Ford of the Itata: the army crosses
stops.campa: The squadrons cross the Itata northward: the river of his childhood captivity, forded now at the head of an army. Lautaro raises the country as he goes, calling the subject Mapuche of the middle valleys back to the war; some come with lances, some hide their seed-corn and pray for him to pass. He marches light and fast in the Spanish manner, remounts driven with the column, scouts thrown far ahead in the Mapuche manner. Behind him Arauco; before him the harvest lands of the enemy. Every ford he takes is a sentence of the conquest read backward.
suggested_refs: The Itata as the old frontier of Valdivia's first entrada

stops.name: Ford of the Maule, beyond every precedent
stops.campa: The Maule: the river the Inca himself could not pass in force, the old wall of the world. Lautaro puts his army across it and the canon holds its breath: a toqui of Arauco operating in the enemy's granary, farther north than any war-party of the nation has ever struck. The promaucaes waver between their promises and their fear; those lands that ride with Santiago he treats as Spain taught him to treat rebels, and the valley learns that the liberator has the conqueror's arithmetic too. Santiago musters in terror. In the toqui's camp the watchword is the name of the city.
suggested_refs: The Maule as the ancient southern limit of the Inca (canonical geography)

stops.name: Peteroa on the Mataquito: the fort raised, Diego Cano beaten
stops.campa: By the Mataquito, at Peteroa, Lautaro plants a pucará in the Spanish fashion improved by Mapuche cunning: earthworks and palisade, the ground before it flooded by cut channels so that cavalry founders in the toqui's engineered marsh. Santiago sends Diego Cano's horsemen to probe; the probe is broken and the survivors carry back the unthinkable report: the Indian general fortifies within striking distance of the capital and beats Spanish cavalry with Spanish works. The groom of Valdivia has become the engineer of Arauco. In Santiago the vecinos arm their households and remember Concepción.
suggested_refs: Batalla de Peteroa
The flooded-ground stratagem in the chronicles
sources: Alonso de Góngora Marmolejo, Historia de Chile

stops.name: Peteroa: Villagra's assaults withstood, the retreat over the Maule
stops.campa: Pedro de Villagra comes up from the south with a real force and hammers the pucará for days. The relays hold the wall; the flooded ground drowns each charge; but the arithmetic of empire grinds on: hundreds of warriors fall to harquebus fire for a handful of Spaniards, and word comes of fresh companies marching from Santiago. Lautaro does what the masters of war call the hardest thing: he breaks off, slips his army out, and retires over the Maule in good order, mauled but unbroken. The Spaniards burn the empty fort and call it victory. Both sides know he will come back.
suggested_refs: Batalla de Peteroa, the fighting retreat
sources: Pedro Mariño de Lobera, Crónica del Reino de Chile

stops.name: The second march north: drought, epidemic, Guacolda beside him
stops.campa: He winters, raises fresh squadrons from a land hollowed by plague, and marches north again: through drought now, the fords low, the promaucae country hostile and picked clean. The army is smaller and harder. And the canon sets a figure beside him on this last road: Guacolda, his wife, whom the poem loves, riding with the toqui through the burnt valleys. Where the first march was a thunderbolt, the second is a pilgrimage of will: he goes because the design is right, because Santiago is still there, because a hawk stoops even through bad air. The country north of the Maule shutters itself and waits.
suggested_refs: Guacolda in La Araucana, Canto XIII
The drought and epidemic of 1556-57 in the chronicles
sources: Alonso de Ercilla, La Araucana, Canto XIII

stops.name: Camp on the Mataquito, under the hill of Chiripilco: the hidden fort
stops.campa: He sets his camp in the vale of the Mataquito, between the river and the wooded hill the country calls Chiripilco: screened, watered, a knife laid quietly against the road to Santiago. From here he raids the valley, burning the estancias of collaborators, gathering the promaucaes who still dare. But the valley has eyes. A picunche of the district goes to the Spaniards and sells the one commodity Lautaro never had to sell about Valdivia: the layout of the camp, the posts of the sentries, the hour when the squadrons sleep. Francisco de Villagra and Juan Godíñez begin a night march through the hills, avoiding the roads.
suggested_refs: Batalla de Mataquito, the betrayal of the camp
Cerro Chiripilco / La Huerta de Mataquito, traditional site
sources: Alonso de Góngora Marmolejo, Historia de Chile

stops.name: The ruca by the rampart, the night of omens
stops.campa: The last night. In the toqui's ruca the canon sets its most tender scene: Guacolda wakes from a dream and tells it weeping: she has seen his end arrived, 'la fin tuya y principio de mi llanto,' his death and the beginning of her mourning. Lautaro laughs the omen away with a soldier's theology: fortune has thrown him down steeper places and he has always climbed out with honor. She will not be consoled; she vows that the sword that parts them will send her after him. Outside, the sentries sleep; the canon says it bitterly. In the dark hills above, armor moves without torches.
stops.quote: En más peligros que éste me he metido / y dellos con honor siempre he salido.
stops.quote_source: Lautaro to Guacolda, La Araucana, Canto XIII
suggested_refs: La Araucana, Canto XIII, the dream of Guacolda
Guacolda in Chilean painting, opera (Ortiz de Zárate) and school canon
sources: Alonso de Ercilla, La Araucana, Canto XIII

segments.name: Mataquito, and the Name That Sleeps

stops.name: Mataquito, the dawn attack and the death of Lautaro
stops.campa: Dawn, 29 April 1557. Villagra and Godíñez burst out of the dark upon the sleeping camp from the hill side, where no attack was believed possible. Lautaro comes out of his ruca at the first cry, weapon in hand (the canon says he carried a partesana that had been Valdivia's), turning to rally the relays as he has turned every battle of his life. He is met at his own doorway: a dart, thrown or fated, takes him through the heart on the left side, and the swift hawk falls at the entrance of his house. He is perhaps twenty-three. The battle is decided in that single fall.
stops.quote: Por el siniestro lado, ¡oh dura suerte!, / rompe la cruda punta y tan derecho, / que pasa el corazón más bravo y fuerte.
stops.quote_source: The death of Lautaro, La Araucana, Canto XIV
suggested_refs: La Araucana, Canto XIV, the death at dawn
Memoria Chilena, 'Muerte a Lautaro'
The partesana of Valdivia in the tradition
sources: Alonso de Ercilla, La Araucana, Canto XIV

stops.name: The field of Mataquito: the army dies around its toqui
stops.campa: The squadrons, headless, do not surrender. They form at the rampart around the body and fight the morning out, and the canon counts the dead in hundreds upon hundreds with almost no Spaniards fallen: a massacre that is also a testament, for not a squadron breaks until it is destroyed. Of Guacolda the poem keeps its promise darkly: the canon carries her out of the burning camp bound to her vow, the sword that made the parting drawing her after him into legend. The Spaniards strip the field. Among the spoils they find Spanish arms, Spanish armor, Spanish horses: the whole curriculum of the stable, returned.
stops.quote: La espada que hará el apartamiento, / hará que vaya en vuestro seguimiento.
stops.quote_source: Guacolda's vow, La Araucana, Canto XIII

stops.name: Plaza of Santiago, the head on the pike
stops.campa: They cut off the head of Lautaro and carry it north to Santiago, and set it on a pike in the plaza, the same plaza his boyhood swept, before the houses of the masters whose horses he groomed. The vecinos come to look at the face of their terror and find it young. The canon reads the pike as Spain reads it: order restored. And reads it again as Chile will read it: seed planted. Vengeance for Valdivia's head, answered head for head; but the head of Valdivia bought a war, and the head of Lautaro buys three hundred years of one.

stops.name: Arauco: Caupolicán takes up the staff; the war that does not end
stops.campa: South of the Bío-Bío the nation does not kneel. Caupolicán, toqui of the log-trial, carries the war on against the new governor Don García; at Millarapue this very year the squadrons close again in Lautaro's relays, and when Caupolicán is betrayed and impaled at Cañete, Ercilla, who watched, writes the empire's own epic around the dignity of the impaled. The frontier congeals on the great river. Arauco domada is a title, never a fact; for three centuries the Bío-Bío remains the one border in the Americas that Spain cannot erase. The method of the hawk becomes the inheritance of every toqui after him.

stops.name: Buenos Aires, the Logia Lautaro: the name wakes
stops.campa: Two hundred fifty-five years. Then, in March 1812, the frigate George Canning drops anchor at Buenos Aires, and José de San Martín steps ashore with Alvear and Zapiola, carrying a secret society for the liberty of America. When they constitute their lodge, the name they give it is neither Greek nor Roman nor Spanish: LAUTARO. The brothers of the Logia Lautarina (San Martín, O'Higgins, the architects of the Andes crossing) swear their oaths under the name of the boy from Arauco who learned the master's warfare in the master's stable and turned it. The hawk, they knew, was the first of them. The circle closes at the beginning.
